title: IF GOD SAID TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH… WHY DID HE ALLOW MEN IN THE OLD TESTAMENT TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES?
paragraphs: IF GOD SAID TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH… WHY DID HE ALLOW MEN IN THE OLD TESTAMENT TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES?

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob married Leah and Rachel. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. Yet Jesus said marriage was designed for two to become one. Was God contradicting Himself—or have we been confusing what Scripture records with what God actually approves?
There is a question that can shake a believer's confidence if nobody is willing to answer it honestly.
And it begins with something Jesus Himself said.
“And they twain shall be one flesh.” — Matthew 19:5, KJV
One flesh.
Not three. Not four. Not a husband collecting wives as though covenant love were something that could be divided without consequence.
One.
Yet open the Old Testament, and suddenly you encounter men who had more than one wife. Some were patriarchs. Some were kings. Some were men God used powerfully in the unfolding story of redemption.
Abraham. Jacob. David. Solomon.
And the uncomfortable question comes rushing in.
If God's original design was one man and one woman becoming one flesh, why did He permit polygamy among His own people?
Was marriage different back then?
Did God change His mind?
Or is there something about the difference between God's perfect design and humanity's fallen condition that we have failed to understand?
Stay with this question, because the answer is not simply about ancient marriage customs.
It is about the terrifying ease with which human beings can become accustomed to something God never intended as His ideal.
It is about the difference between being blessed by God and having every decision approved by God.
And somewhere in this story, we may discover something uncomfortable about ourselves.
Because polygamy is not the only thing humanity has learned to justify while still calling itself faithful.
Before there was a king with a palace full of wives, before Abraham entered Hagar's tent, before Jacob found himself trapped in a household divided by jealousy, there was a garden.
And in that garden, God established something astonishing.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” — KJV
The Hebrew phrase translated “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
Basar means flesh.
Echad means one.
Together, the words describe a profound union in which two people are joined in a new kinship bond, expressed bodily, relationally, and covenantally.
It does not mean that husband and wife literally become one physical organism. Nor does the Hebrew word echad, by itself, mathematically prove that no other relationship could ever exist.
That would be asking the language to establish more than it actually says.
The significance is found in the entire creation account.
God forms the man.
God forms the woman.
God brings her to him.
And the man recognizes her as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh.
The narrative presents one man and one woman, joined together in a union that becomes the foundational pattern for marriage.
Adam does not ask God for additional wives.
God does not present him with a collection of partners.
The woman is not an interchangeable addition to his life.
She is the corresponding partner God provides.
And centuries later, when religious leaders question Jesus about marriage and divorce, Jesus does something remarkable.
He does not begin with the customs of Abraham's household.
He does not appeal to the royal practices of David or Solomon.
He goes back to the beginning.
Matthew 19:4–6 records Jesus saying:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” — KJV
Notice those words.
At the beginning.
Jesus takes His listeners behind centuries of human customs, legal disputes, and broken relationships.
Back to creation.
Back to the intention of the One who invented marriage.
The Greek expression in Matthew 19:5 is σάρκα μίαν — sarka mian, meaning “one flesh.”
And Jesus emphasizes that the two are no longer two, but one flesh.
His immediate subject is divorce, not a direct debate about polygamy. We should not pretend otherwise.
But His reasoning matters enormously.
Jesus treats the creation account as the authoritative foundation for understanding marriage.
He does not suggest that later human arrangements have replaced God's original design.
And that brings us to the part of Scripture that many people find difficult.
Because if monogamous marriage was the creation pattern, why does the Old Testament contain so many polygamous households?
The answer requires us to understand one crucial distinction.
The Bible can truthfully describe something without morally endorsing it.
Scripture records murder.
It records betrayal.
It records slavery, adultery, deception, abuse of power, and devastating failures among people who genuinely belonged to the story of God's covenant.
But the presence of an event in Scripture is not the same thing as divine approval.
God's willingness to work through deeply flawed people is not proof that their every choice reflected His will.
And if we miss that distinction, we will misunderstand not only polygamy but much of the Old Testament itself.
Consider where polygamy first appears explicitly in the biblical narrative.
It is not introduced through Abraham.
It appears in Genesis 4:19.
“And Lamech took unto him two wives.” — KJV
Lamech belongs to Cain's line, and the surrounding narrative portrays a world increasingly marked by violence and human self-assertion.
The text does not explicitly declare that Lamech's marriages caused his violence, nor does it pause to pronounce a specific judgment on his polygamy.
But the placement is striking.
The first explicitly polygamous household appears not in Eden's original marriage account, but in the unfolding story of fallen humanity.
Then comes Abraham.
A man called by God.
A man who believed God's promises.
A man whose faith would become an extraordinary example for generations.
Yet Abraham's household was not free from painful decisions.
God promised Abraham descendants.
But Sarah remained barren.
The waiting became unbearable.
And eventually Sarah suggested that Abraham have a child through her Egyptian servant, Hagar.
Genesis 16:3 says Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham “to be his wife.”

This was not merely a modern-style affair. It occurred within an ancient social world where secondary-wife and concubinage arrangements existed, often involving profound inequalities of status and power.
But the fact that such arrangements were culturally recognizable does not mean the biblical narrative presents them as God's ideal.
And what happened next?
Conflict.
Hagar conceived.
Sarah felt dishonored.
Hagar was treated harshly.
A vulnerable woman fled into the wilderness.
The attempt to secure the promise through human arrangements produced suffering that the household could not simply wish away.
Yet notice something breathtaking.
God saw Hagar.
The woman who had been caught in the decisions of more powerful people was not invisible to Him.
Genesis 16:13 records her response to the Lord who spoke to her, identifying Him as the God who sees.
What a moment.
The God who had made promises to Abraham also cared about the suffering of Hagar.
He did not treat her pain as an insignificant side effect of someone else's spiritual journey.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what that feels like.
To be wounded by decisions you did not make.
To be treated as though your pain is inconvenient.
To wonder whether God notices the people who suffer in the shadows of someone else's choices.
He does.
The God who saw Hagar still sees those whom others overlook.
But God's compassion toward Hagar did not mean that every decision leading to her suffering was righteous.
Divine mercy must never be confused with divine endorsement.
Now consider Jacob.
He loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception, he first married Leah, and later Rachel as well.
The household expanded through the involvement of their servants, Bilhah and Zilpah.
Twelve sons would eventually become the ancestors of Israel's twelve tribes.
Surely, someone might argue, that proves God approved of the arrangement.
But look more closely.
Genesis does not portray Jacob's household as a beautiful picture of peaceful, equal affection.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel struggles with jealousy and infertility.
The sisters compete.
The children become entangled in the emotional wounds of their parents.
And years later, Joseph's story exposes just how destructive family favoritism can become.
God brought His covenant purposes forward through that family.
That is true.
But the fact that God brought good out of a fractured household does not make the fractures good.
Think about Joseph himself.
His brothers sold him into slavery.
God eventually used Joseph's suffering to preserve many lives during famine.
But nobody should conclude that selling a brother into slavery was therefore morally approved.
Joseph himself explained the mystery in Genesis 50:20:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” — KJV
There it is.
Human beings can intend evil.
God can bring good.
And those two truths can exist together without evil becoming righteous.
That principle helps us understand the patriarchal narratives.
God's faithfulness to His covenant does not depend upon the moral perfection of the people through whom He works.
If it did, the biblical story would end almost as soon as it began.
But now comes an even harder objection.
What about the laws of Moses?
Because the Old Testament does more than describe polygamy.
It contains laws addressing households in which a man has multiple wives.
Exodus 21:10 requires that a man who takes another wife must not diminish the first woman's food, clothing, or marital rights.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives, one loved and one unloved, and forbids him from depriving the rightful firstborn of his inheritance merely because of favoritism.
These passages cannot be ignored.
The Mosaic Law recognized the existence of polygamous marriages and regulated certain obligations within them.
That is a stronger statement than simply saying the Bible mentions polygamy.
And it deserves an honest explanation.
In the ancient world, women and children could be especially vulnerable to the decisions of powerful men.
These laws placed limits on conduct that could otherwise leave them deprived of support or inheritance.
But regulation and idealization are not identical.
A law governing an existing social practice does not necessarily declare that practice the highest expression of God's original intention.
Jesus Himself gives us an important interpretive principle.
When questioned about Moses permitting divorce, He responds in Matthew 19:8:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” — KJV
We must be precise here.
Jesus is directly explaining the Mosaic concession concerning divorce. He does not explicitly say in this verse that every law involving polygamy was given for exactly the same reason.
Nevertheless, His words reveal something essential about interpreting biblical law.
Not every arrangement permitted or regulated under the old covenant represented the unbroken ideal of creation.
Sometimes God's law addressed human life as it actually existed in a fallen society.
And Jesus directs His listeners back to what was true from the beginning.
This does not make the Mosaic Law meaningless.
It teaches us to read it within the larger unfolding revelation of Scripture.
We must also face another passage that complicates the discussion.
In 2 Samuel 12:8, the prophet Nathan speaks God's judgment to David and recounts what God had given him, including his master's house and wives.
Some readers understandably ask whether this means God positively authorized David's multiple marriages.
The language is significant and should not be dismissed.
Nathan is describing the royal position and privileges transferred to David, and the passage presents these as part of what God had granted him.
Interpreters differ over whether the reference to Saul's wives means literal marital possession or the transfer of the former king's royal household.
But even if the words are understood in the strongest sense, the passage does not establish polygamy as the creation ideal or command all men to practice it.
The same prophetic confrontation condemns David's taking of Bathsheba and his orchestration of Uriah's death.
David's royal privileges never placed him above God's moral authority.
And the wider biblical testimony concerning kings provides another warning.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” — KJV
The warning is not incidental.
It connects the multiplication of wives with the danger of a divided heart.
Then comes Solomon.
A king associated with extraordinary wisdom.
A man who received blessings and opportunities that few could imagine.
And yet 1 Kings 11:3 records that he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines.
A thousand women in his royal household.
Imagine the political alliances.
The wealth.
The status.
The appearance of unimaginable success.
But Scripture does not celebrate this as the ultimate achievement of biblical manhood.
It tells us that his wives turned away his heart.
The man famous for wisdom became a warning about what happens when desire outruns obedience.
You can possess extraordinary gifts from God and still make choices that lead your heart away from Him.
That should humble every one of us.
Because Solomon's tragedy was not simply that he had too many wives.
It was that his heart became divided in its loyalty to the Lord.
And a divided heart is a danger even to people who have never entered a polygamous marriage.
You can have one spouse and still betray the covenant through adultery.
You can be publicly religious and privately unfaithful.
You can defend biblical marriage with your mouth while destroying your own marriage through cruelty, dishonesty, neglect, or contempt.
You can win an argument about God's design and still refuse to live according to the love and faithfulness that design demands.
This is where the question becomes personal.
Because it is easier to examine Abraham's household than our own.
Easier to discuss Solomon's failures than the compromises we have quietly normalized.
Easier to ask why ancient men had multiple wives than to ask why we sometimes demand God's blessing on choices we have never honestly surrendered to Him.
And then the New Testament brings the discussion into sharper focus.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:31–32:
Read that again.
Paul takes the marriage language of Genesis and connects it to Christ and His Church.
Marriage is not merely an arrangement for companionship, reproduction, economic security, or social respectability.
In Paul's teaching, Christian marriage carries a profound symbolic relationship to Christ's covenantal love.
And how does Christ love His Church?
He gives Himself for her.
He does not exploit her.
He does not discard her when she becomes difficult to love.
He does not treat her as an object to increase His prestige.
Ephesians 5:25 declares:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — KJV
This is not a license for male domination.
It is a call to self-giving love.
The same passage calls husbands to love their wives as their own bodies and places marriage within a Christian life shaped by reverence for Christ.
The Greek verb translated “gave” in Ephesians 5:25 is παρέδωκεν — paredōken, from paradidōmi, meaning to hand over or give up.
Christ gave Himself.
That is the model.
Not possession.
Not entitlement.
Not a competition for power.
Sacrificial love.
And the New Testament consistently presents marriage through the language of husband and wife, including the reciprocal obligations of 1 Corinthians 7:2–5.
Paul also instructs that an overseer must be the “husband of one wife” in 1 Timothy 3:2, with similar language in Titus 1:6.
The Greek phrase μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra can be rendered literally as “a man of one woman.”
Scholars debate whether its primary emphasis concerns monogamy, marital fidelity, remarriage, or a combination of qualifications.
So we should not pretend that this phrase alone resolves every historical question about marriage.
But it certainly fits the New Testament's emphasis on faithful, undivided marital commitment.
And when these passages are read alongside Genesis 2, Jesus' appeal to creation, and Paul's teaching about Christ and the Church, the biblical case for monogamous marriage becomes substantial.
Not because the Old Testament hides polygamy.
But because the whole biblical story must be allowed to speak.
There is, however, another question we cannot avoid.
If a man in the Old Testament had more than one wife, did he somehow become “one flesh” with several women?
This is where careful interpretation matters.
The phrase “one flesh” should not be treated as though it describes a physical substance that can be joined to only one other person by a mechanical law.
Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 6:16 is especially illuminating.
He writes:
Paul applies Genesis 2:24 to sexual union outside marriage.
That is remarkable.
It shows that the language of one flesh has a real bodily dimension and that sexual union carries moral significance even where the relationship does not constitute a faithful marriage covenant.
Therefore, it would be inaccurate to argue that a man could not possibly have a one-flesh sexual union with more than one woman.
Scripture itself gives us reason to reject that simplistic explanation.
The issue is not whether a human being can enter multiple bodily unions.
The issue is whether doing so reflects the exclusive, faithful marriage pattern established at creation and affirmed by Christ.
The possibility of a union does not automatically establish the righteousness of the arrangement.
This is an important distinction.
One-flesh language does not magically make every sexual relationship a God-approved marriage.
Nor does the existence of multiple unions prove that God's original design was intended to be multiplied.
In Genesis, the one-flesh union belongs within the picture of a man leaving his parents and cleaving to his wife.
The Hebrew verb translated “cleave” is דָּבַק — dabaq, which carries the sense of clinging, adhering, or holding fast.
It is a powerful word for attachment and loyalty.
Marriage, in its creation setting, is not presented as a casual addition to someone's life.
It is a binding commitment.
And here is something beautiful.
God's design is not merely about restricting the number of partners.
It is about the kind of faithfulness that makes covenant love possible.
To be known.
To be cherished.
To be treated with dignity.
To be loved without being reduced to a possession.
To be joined in a relationship where faithfulness is not an optional luxury but a sacred responsibility.
Of course, not every monogamous marriage reflects that beauty.
A marriage can have exactly two people and still be filled with betrayal, fear, manipulation, or violence.
A wedding certificate does not automatically produce Christlike love.
And biblical teaching about marriage must never be used to pressure someone to remain in immediate danger or to excuse abuse under the language of submission or covenant.
The God who calls people to faithfulness also cares about justice, truth, and the protection of the vulnerable.
That matters.
Because sometimes people speak passionately about defending the institution of marriage while overlooking the wounded people living inside it.
Jesus never taught us to value religious appearances more than human beings.
And that brings us to the deepest part of this story.
The Bible is not ultimately the story of perfect husbands, perfect wives, or perfect families.
It is the story of a faithful God working through an unfaithful world.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
And so do we.
David's life makes this especially clear.
He committed adultery with Bathsheba.
He arranged for Uriah to be killed.
He tried to conceal what he had done.
Yet when the prophet Nathan confronted him, David could no longer hide behind his throne.
The king had power.
The king had status.
The king had people who obeyed his commands.
But none of those things could erase his guilt before God.
And in Psalm 51:10, David prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — KJV
The Hebrew word translated “create” is בְּרָא — bera, from the verb bara, used for God's creative action.
David was not merely asking for better public relations.
He was pleading for inward renewal.
He needed more than a repaired reputation.
He needed mercy.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us need to pray today.
Not because our circumstances are identical to David's.
But because we know what it is to excuse ourselves.
To justify what we should confess.
To defend choices that have wounded others.
To want forgiveness without surrender.
To want God's promises while resisting His authority.
And then Jesus enters the story.
Not as another flawed patriarch.
Not as another king whose appetites eventually overpower his wisdom.
But as the faithful Son of God.
The One who came to fulfill the Father's will.
The One who loved without exploiting.
The One who spoke truth without hypocrisy.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One whose blood established the new covenant.
At the cross, Jesus did not declare that sin was harmless.
He bore its judgment.
He did not pretend that human rebellion was insignificant.
He gave His life to redeem sinners.
And through His resurrection, He opened the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
That is why the Gospel is greater than a discussion about ancient marriage practices.
Because the same Scriptures that expose the failures of humanity point us toward the Savior who came to rescue humanity.
The men of the Old Testament could not save us.
Their households could not save us.
Their achievements could not save us.
Even their faith, however genuine, pointed beyond themselves to the grace of God.
Only Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And when Jesus redeems a person, He does not simply offer permission to continue living in rebellion without repentance.
He calls that person to follow Him.
To confess sin.
To turn from it.
To receive forgiveness.
To walk in the truth.
To learn a new way of loving.
This is not salvation earned through flawless marital performance.
It is salvation by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, a grace that produces a transformed life.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds those truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not a reward for having an impressive past.
Grace is God's undeserved gift to people who need a Redeemer.
And if you have a broken marital history, hear this carefully.
Your past does not place you beyond the reach of Jesus.
If you have been betrayed, your suffering is not invisible to Him.
If you have betrayed someone, forgiveness is possible through Christ, but genuine repentance also calls for truth, accountability, and a willingness to face the harm you have caused.
If you are single, you are not an incomplete human being waiting for marriage to give you worth.
Jesus Himself lived without marrying, and the New Testament honors faithful singleness.
If you are widowed, divorced, abandoned, or carrying wounds from a relationship you cannot undo, the Gospel is not reserved for people whose lives fit a perfect family portrait.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
And if you are married, remember this.
The goal is not merely to say you believe in biblical marriage.
The goal is to let the Lord transform how you love the person to whom you have made promises.
With truth.
With patience.
With fidelity.
With humility.
With repentance when you fail.
With the courage to seek help when your relationship is wounded.
Because a marriage that looks respectable from the outside can still desperately need the healing work of Christ.
And a broken person who sincerely turns to Jesus can find a future that shame once convinced them was impossible.
So what do we finally do with the question that started all of this?
If marriage means becoming one flesh, how did Old Testament polygamy fit that language?
We answer without hiding the difficult passages.

Old Testament polygamy was a real, socially recognized practice. Scripture records it, and Mosaic law regulated aspects of it. Some men through whom God worked had multiple wives, and their inclusion in the covenant story cannot be denied.
But those facts do not, by themselves, establish polygamy as God's original marriage ideal.
Genesis presents the foundational union of one man and one woman.
Jesus returns to that beginning as the standard for understanding marriage.
The New Testament develops marriage through the language of mutual marital responsibility, fidelity, and Christ's self-giving love for His Church.
And the Old Testament narratives repeatedly reveal the painful consequences that can accompany divided households, favoritism, rivalry, and unchecked desire.
We should be careful not to claim that every conflict in those households was caused solely by polygamy or that every polygamous household was portrayed in exactly the same way.
Scripture is more complex than that.
But its overall movement gives Christians strong reason to understand faithful monogamy as the biblical pattern for marriage.
God's patience with human failure is not the same as God abandoning His design.
And this truth reaches far beyond marriage.
Because every one of us is tempted to ask how much of our own way we can preserve while still claiming to follow Jesus.
How much pride?
How much dishonesty?
How much bitterness?
How much secret compromise?
How much selfishness disguised as freedom?
Yet the invitation of Christ is not to negotiate with the darkness.
It is to come into the light.
Maybe you have been reading this as a theological question.
But somewhere along the way, another question began forming in your heart.
Where have I been asking God to approve what He is calling me to surrender?
Where have I confused His patience with His permission?
Where have I used someone else's failures to avoid examining my own?
And where have I forgotten that the same Jesus who calls me to repentance is also the Jesus who offers me grace?
You do not need to answer those questions publicly to make them real.
But do not run from them.
Bring them before God.
Let His Word search you.
Let His mercy humble you.
Let His truth correct you.
And let the cross remind you that your story does not have to end where your sin left you.
You do not have to reveal painful private details.

And if you have a sincere biblical question or see a passage that deserves further examination, bring it into the conversation respectfully. We should never be afraid to open the Scriptures and search for truth together.

If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them—not to embarrass or accuse them, but because they might appreciate a thoughtful conversation about Scripture and the grace of Jesus Christ.
Not because every person who reads it will agree with every conclusion.
But because difficult biblical questions deserve careful, Christ-centered answers rather than shallow slogans.
A single share may reach a struggling believer, a curious unbeliever, a wounded spouse, or someone who has quietly wondered whether the Bible contradicts itself.
At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to keep making space for that kind of study.
Not merely content that stirs emotion for a moment, but biblical teaching that leads people to read God's Word, examine their lives, repent where necessary, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
Those resources are part of a larger mission: helping people move beyond inspirational moments into a life of genuine discipleship.
It helps sustain the time, effort, research, writing, and resources needed to keep producing Christ-centered teaching and reaching more people with the message of the Gospel.
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, that support can be a meaningful ministry offering—an expression of generosity toward the work of sharing biblical truth.
But let us keep this biblically clear.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, not pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The Scriptures are.
The spiritual growth of people who desperately need truth and grace is.
But they can serve as useful reminders, conversation starters, and resources for Christian living while helping sustain the ministry.
Send it to a friend who loves studying difficult passages of Scripture.
Because we are not building a community around the illusion that Christians have perfect lives.
We are gathering around the perfect Savior who meets imperfect people with truth and grace.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the beginning.
A garden.
A man.
A woman.
A union established by God.
Then centuries of human failure.
Broken promises.
Divided homes.
Kings who had everything and still lost their way.
Families that carried wounds from one generation to another.
And finally, a cross.
At that cross, the Son of God gave Himself for people whose love had so often been selfish, divided, and unfaithful.
He did not come merely to win a debate about marriage.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
And the One who taught us to return to the beginning is also the One who makes a new beginning possible for everyone who comes to Him in faith.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
Not that our past was always righteous.
Not that every choice we made was pleasing to God.
Not that our wounds were imaginary or our sins insignificant.
But that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
So do not confuse the Bible's record of human brokenness with a celebration of that brokenness.
And do not confuse the exposure of your own brokenness with the end of your story.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is possible.
Transformation is possible.
Because Jesus died for sinners and rose again.
The greatest miracle is not that God found faithful people in a broken world—but that the faithful Christ came to redeem people who had broken faith.
